e.t: This word describes something constant and continuous—something that keeps going without stopping or interruption. It can describe an ongoing condition or action rather than something occasional or temporary. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing a focused but consistent use of the word. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is steady continuation.

This word means “disorder”: a condition in which things are not arranged or conducted in an orderly way. It points to a lack of order rather than to one particular event or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Luke, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, and James. Its precise force in any one verse is determined by the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This word means “delivered” or “to deliver”—to hand someone or something over to another person or authority. It describes the act of bringing a person into the care, custody, or control of someone else. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 23:33. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the completed act of delivering or handing over.

This word means “opening,” describing the act of making something open or giving access. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 6:19, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its basic sense remains straightforward: something closed is opened, or an opening is provided. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being opened in that occurrence.

e.t: This verb means “to demand” or “to demand back”—to require something from another person, including the return of what is owed or expected. Its wording points to an active request made with obligation or authority behind it, rather than a casual question. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Luke, so its precise force in either passage comes from the surrounding sentence and context.

This word means a barn or storehouse—a building or place where harvested grain and other goods are kept. It refers to a storage place rather than to the grain itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, in Matthew and Luke. Its uses include both singular and plural references, but the central idea remains the same: a place for gathering and preserving produce. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is part of a farming image, a comparison about provision, or a description of storing a harvest.

This Greek New Testament word means “left” or “left side,” describing position in relation to something else. It identifies the side opposite the right, whether referring to a person’s location or the placement of an object. The word appears four times in the Greek New Testament, each in a different verse. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what person or thing is positioned on the left.

This word means “to domineer” or “to have authority over.” It describes exercising control or authority over another person, with the gloss “to domineer” indicating a forceful or controlling manner rather than simply holding a position of responsibility. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 2:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself concerns taking authority over someone else.

This Greek New Testament word means “by itself,” pointing to something acting, occurring, or existing independently rather than through another agent. It presents the subject as functioning on its own. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, appearing once in Mark and once in Acts. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains independence or action without outside assistance.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 3:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning remains the exercise of governing authority or control.

The word appears in Matthew 23:4, Luke 8:29, and Acts 22:4.

e.t: This word means “to assert” or “to insist.” It describes speaking with firm conviction, emphasizing a claim rather than merely mentioning it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing a repeated but uncommon expression for strongly maintaining what one says. Its exact force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding sentence and conversation, but the central idea remains a confident, emphatic assertion.

This word means “jettisoning” or “throwing out”—deliberately casting something away, often to remove a burden or reduce danger. It describes the act itself rather than the object being discarded. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the purposeful disposal of something no longer retained.

e.t: This word is a preposition meaning “in,” “among,” “at,” or “with,” showing the setting, location, or association connected with an action or statement. It can also express being on, by, or through something, and may introduce a time or circumstance, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament it occurs 2,752 times, so it is a common connecting word rather than a term naming a person, object, or event. Its central idea is connection within a place, situation, group, or circumstance.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its broader range must be understood from its basic sense rather than from many repeated uses. Its precise force in Luke 11:29 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: This word means “to care” or “to take care of” someone or something. It describes active attention and responsible concern rather than merely noticing a need. In the New Testament, it is used three times: twice in Luke and once in 1 Timothy. Its basic sense can apply to practical care for another person, as well as the responsible oversight expected in a household. The surrounding passage determines the specific object of that care, but the word itself emphasizes taking responsibility to look after it.

This word means “readiness”: a state of being prepared, available, or set to proceed. It describes more than willingness in the abstract; it points to a prepared condition that enables someone to respond or act. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 6:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the condition of being ready.

This word means “blackness” or “darkness,” describing a condition marked by the absence of light. It is used five times in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews, 2 Peter, and Jude. The passages consistently use it for darkness itself rather than for a person, object, or action. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a dark or black condition.

Thyatira is a proper name identifying a place. It is not a descriptive word or an action; it names Thyatira wherever it appears in the Greek New Testament. The name occurs four times: once in Acts and three times in Revelation. Because the available material gives the name but no underlying definition, its basic meaning is simply the place-name “Thyatira.” Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and its connection with that place.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to make atonement for” or “to propitiate.” It describes making the necessary provision for sin so that reconciliation with God may be secured. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 18:13 and Hebrews 2:17. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains the act of making atonement or providing propitiation.

The Greek New Testament word means “fish,” referring to an aquatic animal used as food or as an ordinary creature. It is a noun naming fish, whether the reference is singular or plural in context. This word occurs 20 times in the Greek New Testament, across 18 verses, from Matthew through 1 Corinthians. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward; the surrounding passage determines what is being said about the fish.

The word appears five times in the New Testament, in James and 1 Peter, showing a repeated concern with how people speak about others. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense concerns harmful or hostile speech directed toward another person.

e.t: “Laodicean” refers to a person associated with Laodicea. It functions as a name or descriptive term identifying people from that place. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word itself establishes the person’s association with Laodicea, while the wider context would show why those people are mentioned. It does not by itself state a spiritual quality, belief, or action.

The word means “plant,” referring to living growth that comes from the ground. It identifies a kind of growing thing rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing once each in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Romans. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains straightforward: a plant. The word is used across both Jesus’ teaching and Paul’s instruction, showing that it can describe ordinary created growth in different settings.

This Greek word means “wolf,” the name of the animal. In the Greek New Testament it occurs six times across five verses, retaining this same basic meaning. It appears in Matthew, Luke, John, and Acts, so its use is spread across several New Testament books rather than being confined to one writer. The precise force of the word in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “blessedness,” describing the state or condition of being blessed. It names the good fortune or happiness associated with receiving God’s favor rather than describing a person as blessed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Romans and once in Galatians. Its use in these passages connects the idea of blessedness with the condition being discussed, while the surrounding verse determines the specific aspect in view. The same English rendering appears at all three occurrences.

e.t: “Middle” or “midst” refers to a position between or among surrounding people or things. It identifies something located centrally, within a group, or in the space separating others. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs 58 times, so it serves as a general location word rather than naming one particular object or event. Its exact force—whether central position or being among others—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. The word appears from Matthew through Revelation, including references translated “midst” and “middle.”

The word means “thigh,” the upper part of the leg between the hip and knee. It is a concrete body-part term, naming a person’s thigh rather than an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Revelation 19:16; the word’s precise significance there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, not on the body-part term alone.

Niger is a personal name, referring to a man identified by that name in the Greek New Testament. It is not presented here as a description, action, or general quality, but as the person’s distinguishing name. The name occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 13:1. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies Niger plainly and directly.

e.t: This word means “to journey” or “to travel,” describing movement from one place to another. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is straightforward: a person is traveling or journeying along a route.

This word means “vinegar” or “wine vinegar,” a sour liquid made from wine. It is a noun naming a specific drink or liquid rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, with every recorded English rendering using “vinegar.” Its occurrences are found in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The precise significance of the liquid in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word refers to the loins, the part of the body around the waist. It names a bodily area and can be rendered “loins” or “waist.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including descriptions of clothing and references to physical descent. Its basic meaning remains the waist or central midsection, while the precise force in any sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

It occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, each in a different verse. The word appears in John, Acts, 2 Timothy, and Titus, so its central sense remains consistent even though each passage supplies its particular setting.

This word means “little tablet” or “writing tablet,” referring to a small surface on which something could be written. It names an ordinary writing object, not an action or an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 1:63. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains a small tablet used for writing.

Carousing means joining in loud, uncontrolled drinking and partying. It describes behavior marked by indulgence and disorder rather than ordinary fellowship or celebration. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears only once, in 1 Peter 4:3. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to excessive, riotous social pleasure. The central idea is a lifestyle of unruly revelry that a person may leave behind rather than continue practicing.

Prisca is a woman’s personal name, rendered as “Prisca” in the New Testament. It identifies the same person named in Romans 16:3, 1 Corinthians 16:19, and 2 Timothy 4:19. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, each time as a name rather than as a description of an action, quality, or object. Its precise significance in any one reference comes from the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic function is to identify Prisca.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to outrun” or “to run ahead.” It describes moving in front of someone else, reaching a place before them, or getting ahead while traveling. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 19:4 and John 20:4. Its central idea is simple physical precedence: one person moves faster or starts ahead and is therefore in front of another. The surrounding verse determines the exact situation, but the word itself focuses on running ahead or outrunning someone.

This word means the “bow,” the front part of a ship. It is a noun naming a specific area of a vessel rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts 27. The repeated rendering “bow” supports the same nautical meaning in each occurrence. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the forward end of the ship.

This word means “sword,” naming a weapon used as a sharp instrument of combat. It functions as a noun, referring to an actual sword when the surrounding passage presents one and supplying sword imagery where Scripture uses the word in a symbolic setting. It occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, with six occurrences in Revelation and one in Luke. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means an object of worship—something regarded with religious honor or devotion. It is a noun describing what people worship, rather than the act of worship itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts 17:23 and 2 Thessalonians 2:4. These references show that the word can describe a worshiped object broadly, without by itself identifying whether that object is true or false, worthy or unworthy. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “fattened,” describing something made well-fed or increased in physical fullness. It is a descriptive word rather than an action or personal name, and its meaning concerns the condition of what has been nourished. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 22:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing being described.

The word’s basic sense remains focused on the visible convulsing action; the surrounding passage supplies the fuller significance of each occurrence.

This Greek New Testament word refers to “slaughter” or to being slaughtered: the act of killing, or the condition of one put to death. It presents death as something inflicted on a victim rather than as a general reference to dying. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 8:32, Romans 8:36, and James 5:5. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse.

Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the wider context; its central meaning remains the experience or expression of grief. This word means “your” or “yours,” expressing that something belongs to, comes from, or is associated with the people being addressed. It functions as a possessive word, pointing to the relationship between an object or matter and its owners or recipients. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times across 11 verses, including uses in Luke, John, Acts, and several letters. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on what possession or association the surrounding words identify.

This word means “shrinking” or “shrinking back”—drawing away rather than moving forward. It describes a retreating response, whether expressed as hesitation, withdrawal, or refusal to continue. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 10:39. Its central idea is not simply physical movement but the act of pulling back from a course or position. The surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise force there.

This word means “smooth talk”—speech expressed in an appealing or pleasing way. It refers to the manner of speaking rather than simply to the subject being discussed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 16:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to persuasive, polished speech that may sound attractive to listeners.

This Greek New Testament word describes awe or fear—a serious, reverent response that recognizes something greater and weightier than oneself. It can express deep respect joined with holy concern, rather than ordinary nervousness alone. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews 12:28, so its precise force there is understood from that passage’s surrounding words. Its central sense remains a response of awe and fear before what deserves profound reverence.
